after hearing the accounts of what happened, it sounds like this was a tragic accident but one that may have been largely preventable. it is heartbreaking that two lives were lost. admu and its basketball coaching and management team should be held accountable because the incident occurred during an official training activity under their supervision. another concerning detail, as a healthcare professional, is the report that cpr may have been delayed or interrupted. i am trying to understand why transport would be prioritized over immediate, continuous life-saving efforts given that the nearest hospital is reportedly almost an hour away. high-quality, uninterrupted cpr is one of the most critical factors in resuscitating a drowning victim and it should be continued during transport when possible. even in the hospital, when a patient codes during transport, we continue cpr without delay. we either climb on the bed or work alongside it while moving the patient. every minute matters. it is difficult to ignore the feeling that a significant amount of precious time may have been lost in the response. rip rene and divine :folded_hands_light_skin_tone::dove: to the rest of the admu players, i hope you find peace and strength as you recover from this tragedy. may you be surrounded with support as you process everything that has happened.

text: i can still remember that tragic day as if it happened yesterday, and even now, the pain of it stays with me. we were at buguey beach with two of our staff members. it was supposed to be a simple stopover, just a chance to relax for a while. one of our staff decided to go into the water. three stayed on the shore , watching him. he was only about a meter away from the children playing near the sand, and from where i stood, the water looked shallow, no more than knee-deep. then everything changed in an instant. a large wave suddenly hit him. i heard him call out for help, and before we could react, another wave came. he tried a third time to jump up and call for help, but after that, we could no longer see him. the waves just kept coming. we immediately called for the lifeguard, but he was unable to reach him in time. rescuers from the mdrrmo arrived quickly with a life buoy and did everything they could, but they could not save him. divers from santa ana, cagayan were also called, but they were nearly two hours away. by then, what started as a rescue effort had sadly became a retrieval operation. his body was recovered the following day. those hours of waiting were some of the hardest moments. i remember staring at the water, praying, crying, and asking myself over and over how something so terrible could happen so fast. one moment we were all together, and the next, he was gone. the next hard thing is to call his family hoping what just happened was a nightmare.. for a long time, i carried so many questions and so much guilt. i kept wondering if there was something more i could have done. even today, whenever i hear about similar incidents, it brings me right back to that day and the heartbreak we experienced. it is a pain i would never wish on anyone. more than anything, i hope no family ever has to endure that kind of loss. prayers for healing on both side. :red_heart:

text: truth be told, there is really nothing strange about the team-building exercises that the players were asked to do. they are meant to build camaraderie and stamina. the team has been in this place several times before, although some of the players were new to the experience. this is the unpredictability of the place and the sea. the aurora province is facing the pacific ocean where the continental shelf is narrow and therefore more susceptible to wave changes. the locals have a belief that some places have a tendency to collect lives from the unsuspecting - buwis buhay. this happens even in shallow rivers and strangely even good swimmers have fallen victims. surely this may be a form of superstitious belief, but this kind of situation has happened so many times before. often the victims are new to the place. the force that caught the victims is rip current. and its impact is really powerful and its impact is magnified when the affected panics. the fact is the victims really don't know the place that they thought they knew. and even if they knew the place, the place and the situation were really changing. the team didn't think the place was risky, but it was. surely, more safety measures could have been put in place, but when you are at the moment you tend to be overwhelmed. surely no one wanted this to happen. but lessons are learned after the fact. we may advice people not to underestimate the force of nature, but there will always be risk takers and i doubt that this will not happen again to some other people.

activities in the same location created a false sense of security simply because no one had been seriously harmed before. just because a dangerous situation did not result in tragedy in the past does not mean the risk was not there. safety should never depend on luck. there should have been clear safety guidelines, risk assessments, and emergency procedures in place before the activity began. considering that there were multiple coaches and staff members involved, supervision and safety monitoring should have been a top priority. experienced coaches, especially those with many years of leadership, are expected to recognize potential dangers and take the necessary steps to protect their athletes. it is difficult to imagine that any coach would want to see their players placed in life-threatening situations. however, when a tragedy occurs, it is important to examine whether proper decisions were made and whether safety measures were adequate. questions may also be raised about whether there were enough personnel assigned to monitor the activity and whether emergency responders and medical staff had the training, equipment, and knowledge needed to handle a drowning emergency effectively. in critical situations, every minute and every decision can make a difference. as for the teammates, it is important to remember that many of them were reportedly struggling in the same dangerous conditions. during moments of fear, panic, and survival, people may not immediately realize who is missing. the fact that some players remembered divine may be because they had spent more simple apology alone cannot answer all the questions surrounding the incident. a thorough and independent investigation is necessary to determine what happened, identify any failures, and ensure that similar tragedies can be prevented in the future. this situation serves as a reminder to all schools, coaches, and sports organizations that athlete safety must always come first. leadership is not it wasn’t just the coaches who bear responsibility for this tragic incident. the resort and the rescuers also have serious questions to answer. one, there were no proper rescue boats, no jetskis, and apparently not enough life vests or flotation devices available for the athletes. how can you conduct water activities in the open ocean without having the necessary rescue equipment ready? second, the rescuers themselves seemed unprepared. it’s ironic to call them “rescuers” when it shows they lacked the proper qualifications, training, and equipment needed for emergencies. why weren’t there essential life-saving tools available, such as oxygen bags, epinephrine and other emergency medical supplies? what’s even more alarming is the apparent lack of knowledge regarding bls and cpr. based on the accounts being shared, it seems that neither the rescuers nor even some of the coaches fully understood the principles of cpr. why was cpr stopped after only a few chest compressions simply because someone told them to stop? in a drowning emergency, every second matters. it feels like a tragedy that could have been prevented if the staff, coaches, rescuers, and resort management had been properly equipped and trained. if the coaches and players had been taught basic life-saving procedures prior to all the water activities being given, if there had been sufficient life vests, rescue boats, and jetskis on standby, and if proper emergency protocols had been in place, perhaps the outcome could have been different. and after a massive earthquake had already occurred, why was it deemed safe to continue with an open water team building activity in the first place? nakakatanga lang

text: i understand that this was an accident and no one wanted this to happen. but at the same time, it’s hard not to question the safety measures that were in place. the school has been doing this ‘’team-building activity’’ for years and there were already reports before of someone almost drowning. if that’s true, it’s disappointing that more preventive measures weren’t put in place by the coaching staff to avoid a tragedy like this. giving the players a briefing and testing the waters doesn’t seem enough, especially when some of the participants reportedly didn’t know how to swim. they also shouldn’t have been complacent just because the water was said to be “mababaw.” this wasn’t a controlled swimming pool where conditions stay the same. it was open water where currents, uneven depths, and changing conditions can make the situation dangerous very quickly. accidents can happen but when there are known risks and previous warning signs, it’s reasonable to ask whether enough was done to keep the players safe.

text: negligence! even if they had been doing this activity for the past 10 years, that does not automatically make it safe. if the area is known for strong waves, rip currents, or dangerous open-water conditions, then continuing to bring students there is like saying, “let’s see if fire can actually burn.” that is not experience. that is complacency. at some point, if you keep ignoring obvious risks, it stops looking like an accident and starts looking like a failure of basic judgment. as if the coaching staff have a foresight of a potato. i feel bad for all the students involved because the adults failed them. if you are bringing young people into the freaking pacific ocean, there should have been proper safeguards: lifeguards on standby, flotation devices, rescue boats or personnel nearby, emergency medical support, and a clear rescue plan. may briefing kayo about ripcurrents tapos rescue plan at floatters wala? this is what makes it so painful. it feels preventable. these are still kids. realistically, many students will just follow instructions, trust the adults, and go with the flow. they may not feel comfortable questioning a coach, a school authority, or a group activity, especially in a culture where speaking up can easily be seen as being difficult. that is why adult responsibility matters even more. i also wonder if parents were clearly informed about the exact activities planned. if more parents had known the full details, maybe more people would have asked the right questions: is this safe? what are the risks? are there lifeguards? are there flotation devices? what happens if someone gets swept away? sometimes, more eyes mean more foresight. and in this case, that kind of foresight could have mattered. and yes, it is also sad to see other students being bashed, because they are also traumatized. but the pain of rene and divine’s families should not be minimized either. two young lives were lost. if the typical filipino is mad about this news, ano pa yung mga bata na nakita na inaahon yung teammates nila? it's exhausting to see this news on my fyp, but i hope we don't forget it and really push for accountability.

text: some of you ask, "why only speak now?" as if people who witnessed a traumatic event are expected to hold a press conference the next day. they were there. they lost someone they cared about. shock, grief, guilt, and trauma can affect how and when a person is able to share their experience. a delayed statement is not evidence of foul play. stop treating normal human responses to trauma as suspicious simply because they don't fit the timeline you've created in your heads. i'm not defending negligence or saying the school shouldn't be held accountable. but have some compassion for the people who were there too. they were placed in the same dangerous situation, witnessed something traumatic, and lost their teammates. we can ask difficult questions without dehumanizing those who are grieving. these were people who nearly lost their lives. they thought it might be their last moment. and yet here we are, with others saying things like “sana sila na lang” or even sending threats. how low can it get? do you really think you know everyone’s perspective? do you think you’re in a position to judge every intention and every action from behind a screen? comments saying things like "sana si _ na lang."?? that's not seeking accountability anymore—that's cruelty. the surviving players are speaking up now, and people still say, "sabihin niyo kasi yung totoo." but what truth are you willing to accept if you've already decided what you want to hear? it seems like unless their statements match the narrative people have built in their heads, they'll never be believed anyway. you can demand accountability without wishing death on others or treating survivors like they have to earn your empathy. “scripted”? on what basis? because it doesn’t fit the story you already decided to believe? that’s exactly the problem—people form conclusions first, then force everything they see to match it, even without verified information. if there are failures in handling this situation, then yes, those should be addressed at the institutional level, the school, the coaches, the system. but the way some people are turning this into speculation, harassment, and misinformation is not helping anyone. at the very least, use common sense. think critically. please, use your judgment and don’t be easily misled by narratives that haven’t been verified. and regardless of whether this was an accident or not, accountability should still be taken seriously. someone still has to be held responsible for what led to this.
